note: Maps AI Act articles down to concrete verification activities by lifecycle stage, directly reusable as an audit programme.
title: Assessing High-Risk AI Systems under the EU AI Act: From Legal Requirements to Technical Verification
explain_beginner: Europe's AI Act tells companies that high risk AI systems must meet requirements like having a human able to intervene, being technically robust, and using well governed data, but the law states these requirements at a high level and does not say exactly how to check, in a lab or an audit, whether a specific system actually meets them. This paper turns those legal requirements into a concrete checklist. The authors broke eleven broad requirement areas from the law down into 48 more specific sub requirements, and then further into 66 individual, testable verification activities, each tied to a stage of building or running the AI system. An example activity is confirming that a human operator can actually take control of the system while it is running, not just that a manual says they can. The authors are careful to say this is one reasonable way to break the law down, not the only correct one, and that some of the technical standards this checklist depends on were still being finalized in Europe when the paper was written.
explain_business: Any organization placing a high risk AI system on the EU market gets a reusable starting checklist from this paper rather than having to invent a compliance testing plan from the AI Act's legal text alone, 66 specific, lifecycle tagged verification activities mapped back to the law and to standards like ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF that many compliance teams already use elsewhere. The realistic caveat is that the authors themselves call this one reasonable interpretation rather than the definitive one, and note that the European harmonised standards this mapping anticipates were not yet finalized, so a compliance program built on this framework should expect to revise its testing plan once those standards land rather than treating this mapping as the final word. This is directly usable now for scoping an internal conformity assessment program, with the understanding that specific verification steps may shift as EU standards bodies finish their work.
explain_practitioner: The authors decompose eleven high level AI Act requirement categories, covering human oversight, technical robustness, data governance, transparency, fairness, accountability, quality management, risk management, technical documentation, and record keeping, into 48 operational sub requirements and 66 concrete verification activities, each classified by verification type and by lifecycle stage. The framework grounds these activities in an extensive set of existing standards, including multiple ISO and IEC standards, GDPR, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, and ISACA's AI audit guidance, and demonstrates the approach on an automotive intrusion detection system using version controlled artifacts and logged detection events as evidence. The authors state their own limitation plainly, the decomposition is explicitly not an exhaustive or definitive reading of the law, deliberately excludes sector specific rules such as medical device or automotive safety standards, and trades fine grained precision for a technology agnostic mapping that will need revision once the European harmonised standards it anticipates are actually finalized.
